title: Novel Targeted Therapy for Refractory Multiple Myeloma
text: Long-term outcomes of this important and forward-thinking research will reveal whether targeting aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) can prevent recurrent disease progression brought on by cancer stem-like cells and whether traditional chemotherapy can be made more effective in order to increase the proportion of multiple myeloma patients who respond to this treatment. It is possible that this will have a major effect on cancer mortality rates.

title: Whole-Body PET Parametric Imaging for Pediatric Patients
text:
Narrative. Quantitative whole-body PET parametric imaging in pediatric patients remains significantly
challenging and largely undeveloped due to the impracticality of acquiring longer dynamic scans. This project
aims to develop and evaluate a practical parametric imaging approach tailored for pediatrics, which can be
applied to existing PET workflows without prolonging scan time. By enabling safe, efficient, and quantitative PET
imaging for children, this work will contribute to advancing diagnostic precision and improving clinical outcomes
in routine pediatric care.

title: Defining the role of enterococci in reshaping Clostridioides difficile infection
text:
Enteric pathogens are exposed to a dynamic polymicrobial environment in the gastrointestinal tract. This
microbial community is important during infection, but there are few examples illustrating how microbial
cooperation influences virulence of invading pathogens. Here, we propose to define the impact of a group of
opportunistic pathogens, the enterococci, on reshaping the metabolic environment in the gut and influencing
fitness and virulence of the important nosocomial pathogen, Clostridioides difficile.

title: Targeting mechanosignaling in pediatric brain cancer
text:
Public Health Relevance
In comparison to many other childhood cancers, the prognosis of pediatric brain cancers
remains poor. Targeting pathways that relate information from the tumor microenvironment and
serve as intracellular regulatory hubs presents new opportunities for developing innovative
therapeutic approaches, including in pediatric brain tumors. The proposed research will develop
a tunable three-dimensional cell culture platform that is compatible with automated high-
throughput screening for targeting an oncogenic signaling pathway that serves as a central
integrator of information from the tumor microenvironment.

title: Virtual nanostructure simulation (VINAS) portal
text:
The Virtual Nanostructure Simulation (VINAS) database uses novel nanostructure
annotation technique and machine learning approaches. The VINAS web portal will be the first
available online data depository tool to lead the machine learning modeling of nanomaterials to
guide the development of new nanomedicines.

title: Quantitative Analysis Research Core (QuARC)
text: Program Director/Principal Investigator (Last, First, Middle): Stergiou, Nick Project Summary The Quantitative Analysis Research Core (QuARC) emerges as a strategic evolution of the Nonlinear Analysis Core (NONAN), expanding its scope to provide comprehensive quantitative methods necessary for innovative research in human movement variability to treat and prevent motor-related disorders. This transition, driven by MOVCENTR user feedback and our commitment to adaptability, broadens our analytical capabilities beyond nonlinear time series analysis to encompass a wider range of quantitative methods. QuARC will be a unique and nimble resource that supports MOVCENTR investigators through expertise across a broad spectrum of quantitative approaches, including advanced statistical modeling and machine learning, all while retaining NONAN's core competencies. The aims of QuARC are: 1) Expand and maintain a comprehensive suite of quantitative analysis resources to examine human movement variability data, supporting interdisciplinary studies conducted by academic and industrial researchers with the goal of treating and preventing motor-related disorders; 2) Serve as an advanced training and mentoring center for all MOVCENTR investigators, including students and postdoctoral fellows, in applying diverse quantitative methods to human movement data; and 3) Provide expertise for quantitative analysis of human movement data, establishing strong collaborations with researchers at the University of Nebraska at Omaha, throughout Nebraska, the Great Plains IDEA-CTR network, and beyond, while expanding partnerships with healthcare, sports technology, and biotechnology firms. This diversification will increase the QuARC’s impact, visibility, and sustainability, positioning MOVCENTR at the forefront of quantitative analysis in human movement variability research. title: New Von Hippel Lindau (VHL) tumor suppressor signaling in renal cancer
text:
It is imperative to identify new therapeutic targets in ccRCC, which is resistnt towards radio or chemotherapy.
Here we provide evidence for the noncanonical role of VHL on regulating m6A modification and gene expression,
which uncovers new mechanistic insight important in kidney tumorigenesis. This study, if successful, will set the
foundation for therapeutic intervention targeting the VHL-Mettl3/14-m6A signaling axis in ccRCC.

title: Elucidating the relationship between lipid droplets, oxidative lipid damage, and ferroptosis
text:
Ferroptosis is a regulated form of cell death that involves the catastrophic accumulation of oxidatively damaged
lipids. Targeting ferroptosis is a promising approach to treat drug resistant cancers. Our research aims to
understand the cellular roles and regulation of FSP1, a key factor and therapeutic target that promotes cancer
resistance to ferroptosis by generating lipid antioxidant molecules.

title: Clemson University Genomics and Bioinformatics Facility (CUGBF)
text: Genomics and bioinformatics are the currency in today’s Life Science research. A major obstacle for junior faculty from IDeA states is the lack of state-of-the-art facilities and training opportunities commonly found in states with substantial NIH funding. This often hinders the generation of preliminary data necessary to be competitive for NIH R01 funding. The implementation of advanced tools to measure and interpret gene dynamics and genomic architecture is vital to the study of eukaryotic pathogens for the development of therapeutic intervention. Genomic level analyses and bioinformatics are a developing field, with rapidly emerging new standards and technologies that provide insight into the fundamentals of eukaryotic biology. Most life science researchers are not experienced in the use of bioinformatics and genomics. Therefore, we propose the continuation of the bioinformatics specialists hired under COBRE Phase I, hire an additional wet lab technician to handle our rapidly increasing load and then bolster the genomics, computational and bioinformatic infrastructure and educational outreach via the Clemson University Genomics and Bioinformatics Facility (CUGBF) throughout Phase II. The enhanced CUGBF is structured into three complementary parts: 1) a molecular laboratory with genomics and next-generation sequencing (NGS) resources, 2) a bioinformatics laboratory with high performance computing resources, & 3) the personnel and equipment at the Clemson University Center for Human Genetics- Genomics Sciences laboratory (CUCHG-GSL which is supported by a COBRE in Human Genetics). Having all three allows the enhanced CUGBF to offer a comprehensive service package from extraction and next-generation sequencing of nucleic acid to the complex data analysis and interpretation. Through this model, CUGBF has designed, executed, and educated EPIC TIs and CU faculty to enable the integration of genomics and bioinformatics into their research programs. The Primary goal of this COBRE Phase II core enhancement proposal is to continue to enhance the current physical and human capital for genomics and computational infrastructure of the CUGBF and integrate genomic data and computational resources into the TI’s and CU faculty research programs.

title: Investigating siRNA-mediated inhibition of ischemia-reperfusion injury during the liver transplantation process
text:
Liver transplantation is the standard treatment for end-stage liver disease; yet, many procured livers are
discarded due to ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI), perpetuating a vast donor shortage that increases waitlist
times and patient mortality. This proposal seeks to utilize small RNA drugs to silence known mediators of IRI in
liver grafts during the transplantation process. Findings from this study will inform the development of therapies
that increase the number of viable liver grafts, saving the lives of thousands of liver disease patients.

title: Strengthening national food safety system by improving veterinary diagnostics
text:
This goal of this application is to enhance the veterinary diagnostic capacity and capabilities of
Animal Disease Research and Diagnostic Laboratory (ADRDL), South Dakota in support of
improving the national food safety system. This project will allow ADRDL to participate in
Veterinary Laboratory Investigation and Response Network (Vet-LIRN). Through this program,
ADRDL will serve as a regional sequencing lab and also will perform diagnostic testing as required
by Vet-LIRN.

title: Post-Transcriptional Regulation of Tissue Regeneration by RNP-Granules
text:
Humans have limited capacity to regenerate tissues like the heart, central nervous system, and spinal cord,
highlighting an urgent need for new therapies. P-bodies, which regulate the fate of mRNA and control the
expression of one-third of human genes, play a critical role in gene regulation. Our research investigates the
function of P-bodies in tissue regeneration, aiming to advance regenerative biology and inform therapeutic
strategies for development, aging, and cancer.

title: Towards a molecular biology of human olfaction in health and disease
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because it seeks to define human odor-induced alterations
in olfactory cells in normal or diseased conditions. Proposed experiments will combine a biopsy-based
approach and single cell assays to define mechanisms driving olfactory neuronal homeostasis and dysfunction.
The project is relevant to the NIDCD’s mission because it addresses chemosensory disorders in humans.

title: Harnessing cell-to-cell variability to understand viral infection outcomes
text:
While it is now accepted that cell-to-cell variability affects viral infection outcome, we currently lack mechanistic
understanding as to the host factors and transcriptional programs that control it. To gain such mechanistic
insights requires the development of new approaches that are able to connect the cell’s initial state with
infection outcome. This project will develop and apply state-of-the-art single cell approaches to decipher the
molecular mechanisms that control viral infection outcomes at the single cell level.

title: Partitioned polygenic risk scoring and machine learning-derived imaging phenotypes for discovery of novel mechanisms of cardiometabolic disease in people of South Asian ancestry
text:
Cardiometabolic disease – encompassing the obesity-diabetes-cardiovascular disease axis – is increasing
across the globe and individuals of South Asian ancestry have a uniquely high rate of disease representing a
tremendous opportunity for discovery of novel therapeutic targets. Leveraging novel computational methods like
partitioned polygenic risk scoring for genomic data and machine learning methods for image analysis, this
proposal seeks to identify clusters of genes that may be working together to increase risk of cardiovascular
disease. This work could identify pathways that can be targeted by developing precision medicine interventions
for all people who suffer from metabolic and cardiovascular disease.

title: Therapeutic editing to lower PrP in prion disease: Administrative Core
text: Prion disease is a fatal, untreatable neurodegenerative disease caused by the prion protein (PrP). Encoded by the chromosomal gene PRNP and expressed ubiquitously in all mammals, PrP is not pathogenic in its native state, but causes disease when it misfolds into a "prion" capable of conformationally corrupting other PrP molecules. PrP is both the obligate substrate in all prion disease forms and subtypes, and is dispensable for healthy life. Decades of genetic proofs-of-concept, bolstered by recent pharmacologic proofs-of-concept from antisense oligonucleotides, argue that PrP lowering is dose-dependently protective against prion disease, across strains and across a spectrum of disease stages. Accordingly, our program will be oriented around the goal of advancing a permanent, one-time PrP-lowering gene therapy for human use. To drive towards this goal we will pursue three tightly connected Research Projects, each of which will optimize and explore a distinct editing modality for its ability to lower PrP levels in the brain. The structure of the program will allow all three approaches to benefit from access to shared disease-specific models and resources as well as a single Vector Core that will undertake process development, production, and vector characterization. The final determination of our lead project will be made at the end of Year 2 based on side-by-side assessments of potency, dose responsiveness, brain biodistribution, time to effect and durability, off target outcomes, and tolerability, and this decision point will set the course for each project's trajectory in Years 3-5. This complex and dynamic proposal unites expertise across the domains of prion disease biology, development and optimization of genome-editing tools, and viral vector development and production, all of which must be coordinated closely to progress an effective therapy. To ensure that all of these promising pieces synergize effectively, and to guide the overall scientific and clinical mission of the project, the Administrative Core will be charged with rigorous, detailed, and proactive project management. This Core will be led by Dr. Sonia Vallabh, co-led by Dr. Eric Minikel, and supported by a Core Program Manager and Administrative Assistant. The Core will coordinate communication between Projects as well as data, model and protocol sharing with TCDC and the SGCE community. Within the Core we will establish 1) a Project Steering Committee composed of internal principal investigators and 2) a Scientific Advisory Board designed to incorporate the wisdom and realism of seasoned drug developers across sectors, as well as disease-specific clinical and patient perspectives; the Core will ensure regular data-based and strategy meetings to best leverage these resources. Additionally, the Core will lead project administration and governance, provide scientific support across projects, and manage reporting, data sharing and outreach. Success in this program will make a single-dose therapy for prion disease a reality in our lifetimes, and will provide a foundational proof of concept for gene therapy in the central nervous system.

title: Botanical derived progestins and their impact on women's health
text:
Relevance to Public Health
Botanical dietary supplements are widely consumed for the prevention and treatment of
gynecological conditions. Deciphering whether popular dietary supplements contain
progesterone-like molecules capable of regulating progesterone receptor signaling is critical to
ensuring their safe and effective use for women’s health.

title: Mitochondrial dynamics and the control of adipose tissue thermogenesis
text:
Obesity and the associated type 2 diabetes are major public health problems. Understanding how TMEM135
regulates mitochondrial dynamics and brown fat-mediated thermogenesis could uncover a novel option for
treating these metabolic disorders.

title: Networking the parental brain: Transformation of brain-wide electrical networks
text:
As individuals adapt to become parents, vast changes in behavior are needed which rely on brain activity
changes to direct offspring care, etc for survival and adaptive functioning. Previous studies have identified cell-
and region-specific brain underpinnings for parental care behavior, but brain-wide network activity has been
recently found to robustly reflect socio-emotional functions, with computational methods identifying emergent
circuits of relevance to not only specific states but in line in with specific complex behaviors. Here, we will
record brain-wide networks in rodent parents, from pre-conception to post-weaning time points, in conjunction
with video capture of parenting behavior, in the setting of manipulations of hormones and offspring sensory
cues, verified through optogenetic manipulation of circuits, and lastly, across male and females of mono- (Mus
musculus) and dual-parent (Peromyscus californicus) species to capture general and specific signatures.

title: Advancing human biodosimetry with solid-state nanopore analyses
text:
The goal of this U01 project is to develop a biodosimetry measurement system for the rapid assessment of
absorbed radiation dose received in a radiological emergency. We will optimize solid-state nanopore analysis
to measure ionizing radiation effects in three related but independent blood-based DNA markers: direct
fragmentation of mitochondrial DNA, shifts in the characteristic length of cell-free DNA, and changes in the
abundance of oxidative lesions in genomic DNA. We will apply this methodology to determine the dose and
modality of incident radiation in human biospecimens.
